amendments.why: Rule 44's surplus-particle test states two conditions, and the chapter showed that the first is doing work the rule never meant it to do. Every particle the rule itself keeps - matsa' -> *find out*, kanas -> *gather together*, natan -> *put away*, and the *away* of sur -> *take away* - stands beside a verb whose bare English word writes the source lexeme, so 'the bare English verb already writes the source verb's whole lexeme' cannot by itself mark a particle unlicensed; only bo' hiphil -> *bring him back*, where the return is written nowhere in the clause, meets the second condition too. JDG.19 read the two conditions in opposite ways in two verses of one chapter - *away* in *went away from him* `added` at 19.2, *up* in *took her up upon the ass* kept at 19.28 - with nothing in the source to license the difference, and neither verse pass could tell from the rule which reading it wanted. The amendment says which clause the second condition is read against, and keeps every other sentence of the rule as it stood, including the surplus-particle prohibition itself, which now has a boundary a verse pass can apply.
amendments.rule: **A verb the ASV renders as a light verb plus a complement heads on the complement, not on the light verb.** This is rule 31's test applied to a verb: drop each word in turn, and the head is the one whose loss loses the lexeme. `הַאֲזִין` → *Give ear unto* heads on *ear*, because *give* alone gives anything; so too `הִשְׁתַּחֲוָה` → *did obeisance*, `נוֹעַץ` → *took counsel*, `הִמְלִיךְ` → *make king*, `הוֹדָה` → *give thanks*, `כִּלָּה` → *made an end*, `עוּד` → *bear witness*, `חָנַן` → *make supplication*, `בּוֹשׁ` → *put to shame*. The complement need not be a noun: an adjective (`הִכְבִּיד` → *made heavy*, `גָּדַל` → *make greater*) and a second verb (`חָטָא` hiphil → *made to sin*, `אָכַל` → *did eat*) are read the same way. Rule 24's *lexical predicate over subjects and auxiliaries* is about `was gathered`, and must not be read as a preference for the English verb — that reasoning would head *make king* on *make*. **A phrasal particle is not a complement.** `שָׁלַח` → *put forth*, `סוּר` → *take away*, and `נָתַן` → *put away* are one lexical verb plus its particle, and the head stays on the verb; the same subtraction says so, since *forth* and *away* alone name nothing. **But run that same subtraction on the particle before folding it in.** Where the bare English verb already writes the source verb's whole lexeme **and** the particle adds a direction, a result or a repetition the Hebrew does not write, no morpheme licenses that word: it is its own `added` unit under rule 30 and does not join the verb merely because it stands inside its rendering, exactly as this rule leaves a supplied object noun `added` and rule 17 a supplied lexical subject noun. `שׁוּב` → *turn ... again* keeps its *again* with the verb, discontinuous under rule 25, because *turn* alone does not write the returning, and `כָּנַס` → *gather ... together* and `מָצָא` → *find out* keep theirs on the same ground; but `בּוֹא` hiphil → *bring him* ***back*** leaves the *back* `added`, because the hiphil is the bringing and *bring* has already written it. **Both conditions must hold, and the second is read against the whole Hebrew clause and not against the verb alone.** What marks a particle surplus is that it states something the Hebrew has nowhere written, as the return of *bring him back* is: the particles this rule keeps — *out*, *together*, *away*, *forth* — stand beside verbs whose bare English word writes the lexeme quite as plainly as *bring* writes the bringing, so the first condition cannot decide a particle by itself. Where the direction the particle states is written in the clause by a preposition, an adverb or another morpheme, the particle restates what the Hebrew has written rather than supplying what it has not, and it is part of the English phrasal verb by which the ASV renders that verb: it joins the verb's unit, discontinuous around an object under rule 25, and the head is unaffected. `הָלַךְ` with `מִן` → *went* ***away*** *from him* and `לָקַח` with `עַל` → *took her* ***up*** *upon the ass* both keep their particle with the verb, on the same footing as `מָצָא` → *find out*. That the other morpheme holds an English word of its own is not a reason to mark the particle `added`, and it is not an invitation to move the particle onto that morpheme either: the word belongs to the verb's rendering, and a preposition already holding its own English is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw. Read the source verb's lexeme against the bare English verb rather than the shape of the English verb phrase, since the particle of *put forth* and *take away* is what completes a lexeme neither *put* nor *take* writes, and do not fold a surplus particle into the verb, the object or a preposition standing beside it, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and* and rule 51 about a supplied *also*. An ASV italic on such a particle corroborates it and decides nothing, by rule 7. **A supplied object is not a complement either, and that holds of any verb's rendering and not only a light verb's.** Where the ASV writes an object pronoun inside or beside a Hebrew verb's rendering — `וַיַּפֵּל` → *he let* ***it*** *fall*, `וַיַּשְׁקְ` → *gave* ***them*** *drink*, `אֲנִי שָׁמָעְתִּי` → *I have heard* ***it*** — read whether an object morpheme is present. Where one is, it takes the pronoun under rule 18 and the verb keeps the rest, as in `וַיַּעֲבִירֵם` → *caused* ***them*** *to pass through*. Where none is, the pronoun answers to no morpheme, is its own `added` unit under rule 30, and does not join the verb merely because it stands inside or beside its rendering; rule 17's permission reaches a pronoun realizing the verb's own person and number, and never an object the Hebrew does not write, exactly as that rule leaves a supplied lexical subject noun `added`. The verb's unit is discontinuous around such a pronoun under rule 25. **This applies only to a pronoun that truly supplies an object.** A reflexive pronoun the ASV uses to render the Hebrew verb's own voice or its elative sense is part of that verb's unit, because the source verb licenses it: `אִכַּף` → *bow myself* keeps *myself* with the Niphal verb and heads on *bow*, and `הִגְדִּיל עַל` → *magnified yourselves against* keeps *yourselves* with the Hiphil on the same ground. Position inside the English verb phrase is not what makes a word part of the verb's rendering — the complement, or the source verb's own voice or sense, must license it, and an unsupported object does not. **And a pronoun realizing the source verb's own person and number is not a supplied object either, whatever case the English recasting puts it in.** Where the ASV recasts a finite verb impersonally — writing a dummy or anticipatory *it* as the English subject and demoting the verb's own subject to the English object — both words belong to that verb's unit, headed on the lexical verb, exactly as rule 17 keeps a presentative dummy with the finite verb it recasts and rule 21 keeps *it was* with `הָיָה`: `נִלְאָה לַהֲשִׁיבָהּ אֶל־פִּיו` → ***It wearieth him*** *to bring it again to his mouth* gives *It wearieth him* to `נִלְאָה`, while the infinitive and the preposition keep their own English. What the preceding sentences govern is a pronoun denoting a participant the Hebrew never wrote, as the *it* of `וַיַּפֵּל` → *he let it fall* and the *them* of `וַיַּשְׁקְ` → *gave them drink* are; a pronoun denoting the very participant the verb's own person and number denote is not that, and marking it `added` would leave the verb's subject unrendered against rule 2 while an English word plainly realizing it stood unaligned. Test by subtraction as elsewhere — drop the English pronoun and ask whether a participant the Hebrew wrote has lost its rendering, or only one the ASV supplied. Read whom the pronoun denotes rather than the case English puts it in, and read the Hebrew clause before reaching for this sentence: where an object morpheme stands in the clause it takes the pronoun under rule 18 as before, where the ASV writes the verb's subject as an English subject this sentence does not arise, and rule 20's ruling that a cleft or impersonal *it* is `added` governs a verbless clause, where no verb stands to be recast. **A supplied object noun is read on those same terms, and what decides it is whether the English noun writes the verb's own lexeme.** Where the ASV completes a Hebrew verb with an object noun the Hebrew does not write, run rule 31's subtraction on that noun. Where it does not carry the verb's lexeme, it answers to no morpheme, is its own `added` unit under rule 30, and does not join the verb merely because it stands inside its rendering: `לֹא שָׁאָלוּ` → *asked* ***counsel*** *not* leaves *counsel* `added`, because `שָׁאַל` is the asking and *asked* has already written it, and `הָלַךְ` → *go* ***your way*** leaves the supplied noun and its possessive `added` on the same ground, because *go* has written the going and *way* names a path the Hebrew does not write, exactly as rule 17 leaves a supplied lexical subject noun `added` and rule 20 a supplied lexical verb. A supplied noun is not a particle, and the clause-level reading above does not reach it: what that reading keeps with the verb is a word stating a relation the clause writes, and a noun naming a thing the clause never names is not that. Where the noun does carry the lexeme, it is part of that verb's one rendering, joins its unit, and the head goes by the same subtraction to whichever word carries the lexeme: `וַיַּעֲשׂוּ` → *did work* is one unit on the verb, headed on *did*, because `עָשָׂה` is the doing and the working alike and neither English word is a complement the other lacks. Read the source verb's lexeme rather than the English phrase's shape, since this rule's light-verb clause governs where the supplied noun is what carries that lexeme — `נוֹעַץ` → *took counsel* heads on *counsel* — and this sentence governs where the verb's own English word has written it already. A supplied possessive standing on such a noun is disposed of by rule 18's closing sentence and is not made the verb's by the noun beside it. **But a preposition the ASV supplies to reach the verb's own object is part of that rendering.** Where the Hebrew writes a bare direct object — no object marker on it and no preposition of its own — and the English verb reaches that object through a preposition the ASV has written, the preposition belongs to the verb's unit and not to the object noun's: `חָמְסוּ תוֹרָתִי` → *have done violence* ***to*** *my law*, `תְּבַצְּעִי רֵעַיִךְ` → *hast greedily gained* ***of*** *thy neighbors*, `הֵקַלּוּ אָב וָאֵם` → *have set light* ***by*** *father and mother*, `אֲבַקֵּשׁ אִישׁ` → *sought* ***for*** *a man*, `טָחוּ תָּפֵל` → *have daubed ... with untempered mortar*. This is rule 16's reasoning where no marker stands to take the word: the same subtraction test finds that dropping it diminishes nothing but the object relation, and the object noun's own English is the noun. The unit is discontinuous under rule 25 where other material stands between the verb and the preposition, and the head is unaffected — it stays on the lexical verb, or on the complement where this rule's light-verb clause puts it. **And the object so reached may be a pronominal suffix on the verb rather than a noun.** Where a verbal object suffix stands with no preposition of its own and the English rendering reaches it through a supplied preposition — `יִבְּמָהּ` → *perform the duty of a husband's brother* ***unto*** *her*, `יַבְּמִי` → *perform the duty of a husband's brother* ***unto*** *me* — that preposition belongs to the verb's unit on exactly the terms just given, and the suffix keeps only the pronoun rule 18 writes for it. Do not read rule 18's *the English pronoun that realizes it* as reaching the preposition standing beside that pronoun: what that rule places is the pronoun, and a preposition the English verb's valency licenses is the verb's whether its object is a noun or a suffix. Rule 40 does not reach such a suffix either, since no preposition morpheme stands in the clause for the recasting to silence. Test by subtraction as before — drop the English preposition and ask whether anything but the object relation is diminished. Two limits. Where an object marker or a preposition of the object's own is present, that morpheme takes the word under rules 16 and 11, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied reading does. And this does not touch rule 33: a function word supplied for an adverbial accusative is licensed by that noun's own case-function and stays with the noun, whereas a word supplied for a direct object is licensed by the English verb's valency, so read which the Hebrew noun is before placing it.

conventions: A directional particle inside an English phrasal verb stays with the verb throughout this chapter, and only a supplied noun or pronoun is marked `added` beside one. The particle of *went away from him* (19.2), *took her up upon the ass* (19.28), *rose up*, *lifted up*, *sat him down*, *fell down*, *went out*, *go in*, *beset round about* and *brought her forth* is part of the rendering of the verb it stands with, because in each the direction it states is written in the clause or is inside the source verb's own lexeme. The supplied objects are the other side of the same count: *your way* (19.5) and *their way* (19.14) are `added` because *go* has already written halak and *way* names a path the Hebrew does not write, while at 19.27 derekh is written and takes *way*; *her* at 19.25 and *it* at 19.30 are `added` because no object morpheme stands in those clauses, whereas the reflexive *him* of *sat him down* (19.15) and *gat him* (19.28) and the *you* of *get you early* (19.9) render the verb's own sense.

In ha'ish ba'al habbayit hazzaqen (19.22) and ha'ish ba'al habbayit (19.23) the written *the* of *the old man* goes to the article on 'ish, the agreement article on the adjective is unrepresented under rule 47, and ba'al - a construct, which can carry no article - takes a supplied *the* under rule 29. Nothing is fronted from the article on bayit, which takes the *the* standing before its own word. JDG.19.22 was corrected to this division during the verse pass, so a later reader meeting the phrase should not re-derive it the other way.

shakham is headed on *arose* at 19.5 and 19.8 and on *early* at 19.9, and that difference is the ASV's, not a split: *arose early* is a lexical verb with an adverb beside it, while *get you early* is rule 44's light verb, where *get* alone names nothing. The same reading governs lin, which takes *tarry all night* (19.6, 19.9) and *tarry that night* (19.10) whole and heads on *tarry*, with *night* named as the competing head.

Read the source verb's lexeme against the bare English verb rather than the shape of the English verb phrase, since the particle of *put forth* and *take away* is what completes a lexeme neither *put* nor *take* writes, and do not fold a surplus particle into the verb, the object or a preposition standing beside it, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and* and rule 51 about a supplied *also*. An ASV italic on such a particle corroborates it and decides nothing, by rule 7. **A supplied object is not a complement either, and that holds of any verb's rendering and not only a light verb's.** Where the ASV writes an object pronoun inside or beside a Hebrew verb's rendering — `וַיַּפֵּל` → *he let* ***it*** *fall*, `וַיַּשְׁקְ` → *gave* ***them*** *drink*, `אֲנִי שָׁמָעְתִּי` → *I have heard* ***it*** — read whether an object morpheme is present. Where one is, it takes the pronoun under rule 18 and the verb keeps the rest, as in `וַיַּעֲבִירֵם` → *caused* ***them*** *to pass through*. Where none is, the pronoun answers to no morpheme, is its own `added` unit under rule 30, and does not join the verb merely because it stands inside or beside its rendering; rule 17's permission reaches a pronoun realizing the verb's own person and number, and never an object the Hebrew does not write, exactly as that rule leaves a supplied lexical subject noun `added`. The verb's unit is discontinuous around such a pronoun under rule 25. **This applies only to a pronoun that truly supplies an object.** A reflexive pronoun the ASV uses to render the Hebrew verb's own voice or its elative sense is part of that verb's unit, because the source verb licenses it: `אִכַּף` → *bow myself* keeps *myself* with the Niphal verb and heads on *bow*, and `הִגְדִּיל עַל` → *magnified yourselves against* keeps *yourselves* with the Hiphil on the same ground. Position inside the English verb phrase is not what makes a word part of the verb's rendering — the complement, or the source verb's own voice or sense, must license it, and an unsupported object does not. **And a pronoun realizing the source verb's own person and number is not a supplied object either, whatever case the English recasting puts it in.** Where the ASV recasts a finite verb impersonally — writing a dummy or anticipatory *it* as the English subject and demoting the verb's own subject to the English object — both words belong to that verb's unit, headed on the lexical verb, exactly as rule 17 keeps a presentative dummy with the finite verb it recasts and rule 21 keeps *it was* with `הָיָה`: `נִלְאָה לַהֲשִׁיבָהּ אֶל־פִּיו` → ***It wearieth him*** *to bring it again to his mouth* gives *It wearieth him* to `נִלְאָה`, while the infinitive and the preposition keep their own English. What the preceding sentences govern is a pronoun denoting a participant the Hebrew never wrote, as the *it* of `וַיַּפֵּל` → *he let it fall* and the *them* of `וַיַּשְׁקְ` → *gave them drink* are; a pronoun denoting the very participant the verb's own person and number denote is not that, and marking it `added` would leave the verb's subject unrendered against rule 2 while an English word plainly realizing it stood unaligned. Test by subtraction as elsewhere — drop the English pronoun and ask whether a participant the Hebrew wrote has lost its rendering, or only one the ASV supplied. Read whom the pronoun denotes rather than the case English puts it in, and read the Hebrew clause before reaching for this sentence: where an object morpheme stands in the clause it takes the pronoun under rule 18 as before, where the ASV writes the verb's subject as an English subject this sentence does not arise, and rule 20's ruling that a cleft or impersonal *it* is `added` governs a verbless clause, where no verb stands to be recast. **A supplied object noun is read on those same terms, and what decides it is whether the English noun writes the verb's own lexeme.** Where the ASV completes a Hebrew verb with an object noun the Hebrew does not write, run rule 31's subtraction on that noun. Where it does not carry the verb's lexeme, it answers to no morpheme, is its own `added` unit under rule 30, and does not join the verb merely because it stands inside its rendering: `לֹא שָׁאָלוּ` → *asked* ***counsel*** *not* leaves *counsel* `added`, because `שָׁאַל` is the asking and *asked* has already written it, and `הָלַךְ` → *go* ***your way*** leaves the supplied noun and its possessive `added` on the same ground, because *go* has written the going and *way* names a path the Hebrew does not write, exactly as rule 17 leaves a supplied lexical subject noun `added` and rule 20 a supplied lexical verb. A supplied noun is not a particle, and the clause-level reading above does not reach it: what that reading keeps with the verb is a word stating a relation the clause writes, and a noun naming a thing the clause never names is not that. Where the noun does carry the lexeme, it is part of that verb's one rendering, joins its unit, and the head goes by the same subtraction to whichever word carries the lexeme: `וַיַּעֲשׂוּ` → *did work* is one unit on the verb, headed on *did*, because `עָשָׂה` is the doing and the working alike and neither English word is a complement the other lacks. Read the source verb's lexeme rather than the English phrase's shape, since this rule's light-verb clause governs where the supplied noun is what carries that lexeme — `נוֹעַץ` → *took counsel* heads on *counsel* — and this sentence governs where the verb's own English word has written it already. A supplied possessive standing on such a noun is disposed of by rule 18's closing sentence and is not made the verb's by the noun beside it. **But a preposition the ASV supplies to reach the verb's own object is part of that rendering.** Where the Hebrew writes a bare direct object — no object marker on it and no preposition of its own — and the English verb reaches that object through a preposition the ASV has written, the preposition belongs to the verb's unit and not to the object noun's: `חָמְסוּ תוֹרָתִי` → *have done violence* ***to*** *my law*, `תְּבַצְּעִי רֵעַיִךְ` → *hast greedily gained* ***of*** *thy neighbors*, `הֵקַלּוּ אָב וָאֵם` → *have set light* ***by*** *father and mother*, `אֲבַקֵּשׁ אִישׁ` → *sought* ***for*** *a man*, `טָחוּ תָּפֵל` → *have daubed ... with untempered mortar*. This is rule 16's reasoning where no marker stands to take the word: the same subtraction test finds that dropping it diminishes nothing but the object relation, and the object noun's own English is the noun. The unit is discontinuous under rule 25 where other material stands between the verb and the preposition, and the head is unaffected — it stays on the lexical verb, or on the complement where this rule's light-verb clause puts it. **And the object so reached may be a pronominal suffix on the verb rather than a noun.** Where a verbal object suffix stands with no preposition of its own and the English rendering reaches it through a supplied preposition — `יִבְּמָהּ` → *perform the duty of a husband's brother* ***unto*** *her*, `יַבְּמִי` → *perform the duty of a husband's brother* ***unto*** *me* — that preposition belongs to the verb's unit on exactly the terms just given, and the suffix keeps only the pronoun rule 18 writes for it. Do not read rule 18's *the English pronoun that realizes it* as reaching the preposition standing beside that pronoun: what that rule places is the pronoun, and a preposition the English verb's valency licenses is the verb's whether its object is a noun or a suffix. Rule 40 does not reach such a suffix either, since no preposition morpheme stands in the clause for the recasting to silence. Test by subtraction as before — drop the English preposition and ask whether anything but the object relation is diminished. Two limits. Where an object marker or a preposition of the object's own is present, that morpheme takes the word under rules 16 and 11, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied reading does. And this does not touch rule 33: a function word supplied for an adverbial accusative is licensed by that noun's own case-function and stays with the noun, whereas a word supplied for a direct object is licensed by the English verb's valency, so read which the Hebrew noun is before placing it.
amended.why: Rule 44's surplus-particle test states two conditions, and the chapter showed that the first is doing work the rule never meant it to do. Every particle the rule itself keeps - matsa' -> *find out*, kanas -> *gather together*, natan -> *put away*, and the *away* of sur -> *take away* - stands beside a verb whose bare English word writes the source lexeme, so 'the bare English verb already writes the source verb's whole lexeme' cannot by itself mark a particle unlicensed; only bo' hiphil -> *bring him back*, where the return is written nowhere in the clause, meets the second condition too. JDG.19 read the two conditions in opposite ways in two verses of one chapter - *away* in *went away from him* `added` at 19.2, *up* in *took her up upon the ass* kept at 19.28 - with nothing in the source to license the difference, and neither verse pass could tell from the rule which reading it wanted. The amendment says which clause the second condition is read against, and keeps every other sentence of the rule as it stood, including the surplus-particle prohibition itself, which now has a boundary a verse pass can apply.

report: One real cross-verse split. A phrasal particle standing beside a verb whose bare English word already writes the source lexeme was analysed two ways: JDG.19.2 marked the *away* of vattelekh me'itto -> *went away from him* `added` under rule 44's surplus-particle test, while JDG.19.28 kept the *up* of vayyiqqacheha 'al-hachamor -> *took her up upon the ass* inside laqach's unit. The two clauses are the same shape - bare verb writes the lexeme, the particle states a direction, and a written preposition beside it carries that same relation under an English word of its own - and nothing in the source licenses the difference.

Resolved in favour of keeping the particle with its verb: JDG.19.2 is patched and JDG.19.28 stands. Rule 44's surplus test has two conditions, and the second is that the particle add a direction, a result or a repetition the Hebrew does not write. The *back* of bo' hiphil -> *bring him back* supplies a return nothing in that clause writes; *away* restates the separation me'itto writes and *up* the mounting 'al-hachamor writes, each of which the ASV has rendered in its own word. The rule's own kept examples - matsa' -> *find out*, kanas -> *gather together*, natan -> *put away* - are every one of them a particle beside a verb whose bare English writes the lexeme, so the first condition alone cannot be what marks a particle surplus. Rule 44 is amended to say which clause the second condition is read against.

Checked and cleared as context-licensed rather than split: the waw's connectives (*And*, *but*, *so*, *So*, *then*, *Then*, *now*, *for*, *with*, *also*, *Yet*, *that*, *when*, *who*, *which*), read off the ASV under rule 14, with the unrepresented ones at 19.3, 19.7, 19.9, 19.11, 19.22, 19.29 and 19.30 each answering to a clause the ASV opens bare; the hayah frames, where the apodosis waw takes *that* at 19.1 and 19.5 while the frame keeps it at 19.30 because the ASV writes it ahead of the subject clause (rule 45); the three-article phrase ha'ish ba'al habbayit, divided identically at 19.22 and 19.23; 'avi hanna'arah as *the father of the damsel* at 19.3 against *the damsel's father* at 19.4-19.9, both rule 29's count of written determiners; the existential 'ayin, headed on the negation word in all five places; and the object marker, which takes *to* at 19.18 because the ASV spends a word on the object relation and is unrepresented wherever it writes the object bare.

Also cleared: the supplied nouns after halak. *your way* (19.5) and *their way* (19.14) are `added` because *go*/*went* has already written the lexeme and *way* names a path the Hebrew does not write, while at 19.27 derekh is written and *way* is aligned to it. That is rule 44's supplied-object-noun clause, and it is a different test from the particle one - which is why *away* now stays with the verb in the same chapter that leaves *way* outside it.

BSB: no genuine error. The bulk of the 47 disagreements are the documented convention differences on Td (22), C (9), R (8) and To (4), where BSB attaches the morpheme to its host word. The four singletons are the contract as written: 19.9 the suffix of le'ohalekha, whose preposition and noun fuse as *home* and for which the ASV writes no pronoun (rules 30, 40); 19.21 the dative la- before a bare English indirect object (rule 40); 19.29 the suffix of la'atsameiha, for which the ASV writes no possessive in *limb by limb* (rules 18, 22); and 19.30 the reflexive dative lakhem, rendered by nothing at all (rule 40).

Considered and left standing, each a single occurrence whose competing reading its own unit note already names: *Behold here is* on hinneh at 19.24 (the alternative puts *here is* on the presented nominal); the head of *the young man* on *young* at 19.19; and 19.25's *began to spring*, where the aspectual auxiliary is read as part of the infinitive's rendering.
